data.title: Veteran Brokers Join Cushman & Wakefield’s Denver Office to Form Institutional Capital Markets Team
data.description:
Cushman & Wakefield continues to strengthen its institutional and private capital sales capabilities with the addition of Tim Richey, Cartter Berg, and Jack Richey to the firm’s Denver office.

This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261119954607/en/

Tim Richey

In partnership with existing capital markets professionals, they will form Cushman & Wakefield’s institutional capital markets team in Denver, working to expand the firm’s office and multifamily investment sales capabilities across the Mountain West region.

“We’re extremely pleased to welcome a team of this caliber to bolster our capital markets platform. Tim, Cartter and Jack bring exceptional transaction experience, deep institutional relationships and a comprehensive understanding of the region’s investment landscape,” said Miles Treaster, President, Americas Capital Markets at Cushman & Wakefield. “Their addition reinforces our commitment to investors and owners, both across the Mountain West and beyond, as we connect global clients with local experts to achieve their objectives.”

Tim Richey and Berg will partner with Aaron Johnson, Executive Director in Denver, to lead institutional office sales and with Pat Knowlton, Executive Director in Colorado Springs, to lead institutional multifamily sales. Jack Richey will support both product types alongside the broader Denver capital markets team.

“As capital markets conditions evolve, investors are looking for ways to take advantage of the next cycle. Denver is well positioned for continued growth, and we see a strong opportunity to expand our presence in the market,” said Steve Schwab, Managing Principal of Cushman & Wakefield’s Denver office. “Tim, Cartter and Jack bring the experience and relationships to help us do that. Working alongside Aaron Johnson, Pat Knowlton and our broader team, they’ll strengthen our ability to serve institutional clients across the office and multifamily sectors.”

Tim Richey returns to Cushman & Wakefield as Executive Vice Chair and is widely recognized as one of the Rocky Mountain Region's leading institutional office capital markets advisors. Over his 30-plus year-career, he has closed more than $20 billion in transaction value and advised on approximately 70% of the high-rise office sales across the Denver skyline.

Most recently, he served as Executive Vice Chairman with Newmark's Capital Markets division in Denver, following previous leadership roles at CBRE, Cushman & Wakefield and Grubb & Ellis. His return brings deep market expertise, longstanding client relationships and a proven track record of delivering outstanding results for institutional investors across Colorado and the broader region.

Cartter joins as Executive Managing Director and brings more than 16 years of experience across investment sales, joint ventures and capital markets advisory. He has completed more than $20 billion in transactions spanning office, multifamily, life science, retail and hospitality assets throughout the Mountain West and beyond. Cartter previously led acquisitions at BMC Investments and prior to that spent 14 years with Eastdil Secured, where he helped establish the firm's Denver office and advised institutional investors across the western United States.

Jack Richey joins as Director and brings nearly seven years of investment sales experience spanning office, multifamily, industrial, land, and debt and structured finance. Over the past three years, he has been directly involved in more than $600 million in transactions.

About Cushman & Wakefield:

Cushman & Wakefield () is a leading global commercial real estate services firm for occupiers and investors with approximately 53,000 employees in over 350 offices and nearly 60 countries. In 2025, the firm reported revenue of $10.3 billion across its core service lines of Services, Leasing, Capital markets, and Valuation and other. Built around the belief that Better never settles, the firm receives numerous industry and business accolades for its award-winning culture. For additional information, visit www.cushmanwakefield.com.

data.title: Belite Bio Shares Drop After FDA Extends Review Period for Tinlarebant
data.description:
By Chris Wack

Belite Bio shares dropped after the company said the Food and Drug Administration has extended the review period for the New Drug Application for tinlarebant, used for the treatment of Stargardt disease type 1, by three months,

The stock was 16% lower, at $127.11, in morning trade, and is down 20% year-to-date.

The clinical-stage drug development company said the extended Prescription Drug User Fee Act action date is now May 12, 2027.

If no major deficiencies are identified during the FDA's ongoing review, the FDA plans to communicate proposed labeling requests and any anticipated postmarketing requirement requests, if necessary, with the company by April 12, 2027.

Belite Bio said the extension provides the FDA with additional time to review information provided in support of the NDA.

The company said it is confident in the clinical evidence supporting tinlarebant and its potential to address the significant unmet medical need in the STGD1 patient population.

data.title: Consumer Sentiment Climbed in November
data.description:
By Matt Grossman

Consumer sentiment improved in November, according to the University of Michigan's monthly survey, yet it remains near historically low levels that reflect Americans' widespread economic frustrations.

The survey's sentiment index ended November at 51.5, a rise from 48 in October. That also was an improvement from the preliminary November reading of 51 published earlier this month.

Stock-market volatility dented the mood among wealthier Americans who own more assets, said Joanne Hsu, the survey's director. By contract, sentiment improved among low- and middle-wealth consumers.

Democrats and independents reported brighter economic expectations after this month's blue-wave midterm elections rebuked Republicans' economic stewardship. Republicans reported a decline in economic expectations.

data.description:
Key points:
  • US equity indexes mixed; Dow gains, Nasdaq lower
  • STOXX 600 index slides >1.5%
  • Dollar falls; gold down >2%; US crude slips; bitcoin edges up
  • US 10-year Treasury yield falls to ~4.96%

ROTATION, ROTATION, ROTATION

US stocks are showing signs of stabilizing following a sharp selloff in the prior session and a weaker open, although the Nasdaq remains under considerable selling pressure as technology shares continue to slump.

The S&P 500 tech index is the sole decliner of the 11 major S&P 500 CBOE:SPX sectors on the day, on pace for its sixth drop in the past seven sessions, and is now down nearly 7% on the week.

Meanwhile, the defensive consumer staples sector is among the best performers, both on the session and for the week, showing a drop of less than 1% in a week the broader S&P index has tumbled about 5%.

In addition, the Cboe Volatility Index , an options-based indicator that measures expected 30-day stock market swings in either direction, though it is primarily driven by demand for protection against market drops, turned lower on the day after climbing to 31.59, its highest intraday level since March 27.

The shift away from tech has also helped buoy the Dow industrials , with the price-weighted average getting a lift from the nearly 5% gain in UnitedHealth , which was upgraded to a "buy" from a "hold" rating by TD Cowen, which also boosted its price target on the stock to $455 from $402 per share.

On the economic front, the University of Michigan's Surveys of Consumers said its Consumer Sentiment Index climbed to a final reading of 51.5 this month, matching the estimate of economists polled by Reuters, and an improvement from the 51.0 preliminary reading.

data.title: Myanmar genocide judgment may bolster Gaza case against Israel
data.description:
Key points:
  • ICJ finds Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya
  • Judges say genocide can coexist with military aims
  • South Africa says ruling sets important precedent for state genocide

By Anthony Deutsch and Stephanie van den Berg

The International Court of Justice's landmark ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya will strengthen South Africa's genocide case against Israel over the war in Gaza, legal experts said, establishing a precedent that genocidal intent can coexist with a military objective.

While the conflicts in Gaza and Myanmar are legally distinct, both cases before the World Court are based on allegations that states breached their obligations under the 1948 Genocide Convention.

On Thursday, the court found that Myanmar had violated the convention on multiple grounds stemming from mistreatment of the Muslim Rohingya minority by the armed forces.

South Africa, which has brought a genocide case against Israel over its conduct in Gaza, welcomed the judgment. Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola said it set an important precedent by establishing for the first time that a state had committed genocide. He said it was of "great significance" to the case against Israel, which is not expected to be argued until 2029.

Both Myanmar and Israel have defended the actions of their armed forces as legitimate responses to insurgencies. But a majority of nine judges on the 15-member bench found that around 10,000 killings, including of children, the razing of homes, widespread sexual violence and the forced exodus of more than 700,000 people in 2017 amounted to state-sponsored genocide.

The ruling also handed other major legal victories to Gambia, which brought the case seven years ago on behalf of Muslim-majority countries.

The judges found that Myanmar had failed in its obligation to prevent genocide and said it must facilitate the return of Rohingya refugees and pay unspecified reparations.

The court also adopted conclusions from UN fact-finding reports, including one stating that mass deaths and rapes showed genocidal intent.

IMPORTANT PRECEDENT

Israeli legal scholar Yuval Shany said the ruling could broaden the arguments available to South Africa in its case against Israel.

He said the court maintained a requirement that genocidal intent be the “only reasonable inference,” but expanded the contextual factors it can consider beyond a pattern of conduct, to include the scale and systematic nature of acts and the history of persecution.

The approach “gives South Africa more avenues to argue for genocide” in Gaza, Shany said.

Proving genocide is notoriously difficult because it requires establishing an "intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group, as such."

Five criminal acts can constitute genocide: killing members of a group, causing them serious bodily or mental harm, creating conditions calculated to destroy them, preventing births, or forcibly transferring children to ​other groups.

Lamola said South Africa would study the judgment carefully with a view to demonstrating, as the court had in the Rohingya case, that a state's actions, including ethnic cleansing, the killing of children, sexual violence and destruction of civilian infrastructure, can fall within the definition of genocide.

TARGETING OF CHILDREN, WOMEN

Another aspect of the ruling that could resonate in the Israel case was the court's emphasis on the systematic nature and scale of the crimes committed in Myanmar, said Marieke de Hoon, professor of international criminal law at the University of Amsterdam.

South Africa alleges that Israel's military operations created conditions intended to prevent births and disproportionately affected women and children in Gaza. In its filing to the ICJ, it said an estimated 70% of those killed were non-combatants. Israel rejects those allegations and says its operations have been conducted in accordance with international law.

"Arguments that a military intent or military objective would erase the idea that there could be a genocide intent are now rejected by the court," said De Hoon.

She said the judges found that some acts, including attacks on children and women and sexual violence, could not be explained by military objectives alone, leaving genocide as the only reasonable inference.

The Hague Initiative for International Cooperation (Thinc), a think tank funded by pro-Israeli groups, said the judgment would fundamentally alter how courts assess allegations of genocide by imposing a "lower threshold for proving genocidal intent, with serious consequences for Western militaries engaged in confronting terror," such as after Hamas' October 7, 2023 attack on Israel.

It is "not only a verdict in a particular case but a template," Thinc's director, Andrew Tucker, wrote in a reaction.

"Its propositions will be used in future cases: that genocidal intent may coexist with legitimate military objectives...that UN reports compiled without access can carry decisive weight; and that a state can breach the duty to prevent genocide without any finding that genocide occurred."

While the World Court judgment unequivocally found Myanmar responsible for genocide, proving the crime in court remains difficult, said Richard Horsey, senior adviser for Asia at the International Crisis Group.

"The ICJ has never before found that a state committed genocide. The legal bar is extremely high, but what this case shows is that it is surmountable,” he said.

data.title: IRDAI slaps ₹2 cr penalty on Star Health & Allied Insurance
data.description:
The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) has imposed a ₹2 crore penalty on Star Health and Allied Insurance Company for declining some health insurance claims related to Covid-19 on untenable grounds.

In an inspection conducted earlier, the Authority further found that the insurer had made deductions which were not supported by the policy terms, and in many sampled cases, the amount was paid only after the Authority highlighted them,’’ the insurance regulator said in an order issued on Friday.

Policyholders were not informed of the specific policy conditions under which claims were repudiated or reduced, depriving them of an informed basis to challenge these decisions.

The Authority has imposed a total penalty of ₹2 crore under Section 102 of the Insurance Act, 1938, comprising ₹2 crore for violation of various regulations related to claims and the third party administration, among others.

The insurer has also been warned for not ensuring that discounts agreed with network hospitals are reflected in hospital bills and made known to policyholders and was directed to ensure that its claim settlement letters itemise all allowed, disallowed, non-payable and discount amounts and the reduction in Sum Insured.

It was further cautioned for collecting renewal premium more than 90 days in advance and for not providing Insurance Ombudsman details to complainants, IRDAI said.
